slides.title: Two different ways to fail on new data
slides.notes: Students mix these up constantly. Overfitting is a training problem; extrapolation is a data problem.

runs.text: Two different ways to fail on new data
The network has memorised its examples, noise included.
It fails on new inputs that lie inside the range it was trained on.
Cause: too many weights for the data, or training for too long.
The network is asked about a situation it never saw.
It may be an excellent fit everywhere it has data.
Cause: the data did not cover real use.
No error figure warns you, because the validation and test sets have the same gap.
Different causes, different cures. Decide which one you have before changing anything.

slides.title: Overfitting: the curve that tries too hard
slides.notes: The network has enough freedom to fit the measurement noise, and nothing stops it from doing so.

runs.text: Overfitting: the curve that tries too hard
A battery estimator with 30 noisy readings
The red curve passes through every reading, so its training error is nearly zero.
Between readings it swings by 30 minutes or more.
A phone showing "2 h left", then "2 h 40 min", then "1 h 50 min" as charge falls has this problem.
The smooth grey curve has a higher training error and is far more useful.

runs.text: Other signs of overfitting: very large weights, and a fit that changes shape with every random start.

slides.title: Four cures for overfitting
slides.notes: Ask which cure they would use with 40 data points (regularisation, since early stopping would cost them 6 of the 40 for validation).

runs.text: Stop when the validation error turns upward and keep the best weights. Simple, and the usual first choice.
Add the sum of squared weights to the error. Smooth by design, and needs no validation set.
Remove the spare freedom. Risk: too few, and the network underfits.
With enough examples per weight there is no room to memorise. The best cure, when you can get it.
A committee of networks also helps: the wiggles of the members differ and partly cancel.

slides.title: Extrapolation: autumn data, winter question
slides.notes: This is the planned break-and-fix. The fix is to add a full year of data, after which the same network works.

series.name: Network trained on Aug to Nov only

ops.xTitle: Month (illustrative figures for a north Indian city)

runs.text: Perfect on four months, absurd on the next four
From August to November the network matches the data almost exactly.
It has only ever seen temperature falling, so it keeps falling: 0 °C in February.
Nothing in its data says that winter ends.
More neurons, more training or regularisation would not help. Only data from those months would.

slides.title: Novelty detection: know when not to answer
slides.notes: Hagan suggests a companion network trained to recognise the region covered by the training data. Disagreement inside a committee is another practical signal.

runs.text: Novelty detection: know when not to answer
Store the minimum and maximum of every input in the training set. Flag any new input that falls outside.
Measure the distance from the new input to the nearest training examples. Far from all of them means the combination is new, even if each value alone is in range.
What to do with a flag
Do not show the output as if it were reliable. Fall back to a safe rule, ask a person, and log the case as new training data.
A network always produces a number. Novelty detection adds the missing output: "I have not seen this before."

slides.title: Case study 1: a smart position sensor
slides.notes: The idea of a smart sensor: one or more ordinary sensors, with a network that turns their raw readings into the quantity you want.

runs.text: Case study 1: a smart position sensor
Function approximation: two voltages in, one position out
An object between a light and two solar cells casts a shadow. Its position changes the two voltages.
The relationship is smooth but nonlinear, and hard to write as a formula.
A network learns the inverse: from (v₁, v₂) back to the position y.
A cheap sensor plus a small network gives an accurate, calibrated instrument.

slides.title: Case study 2: estimating a probability
slides.notes: The targets themselves are noisy: 50 trials give fractions in steps of 2%. The network pools information from neighbouring conditions and so smooths that noise.

runs.text: Three outcomes, three probabilities that sum to 1
In making synthetic diamond, a carbon dimer strikes the surface. It may bond, bounce off, or bond and later leave.
Which one happens is random. Only the probabilities depend on the collision conditions.
Each condition was simulated 50 times; the targets are the observed fractions.
The softmax output makes the three estimates positive and sum to 1.

slides.notes: The last row of the twin is calibration: a probability estimate is good if events rated 70% happen about 70% of the time. Take the exact training settings from the chapter.

slides.title: Why use a network to estimate a probability?
slides.notes: The published work behind the Hagan chapter reports that the network reduced the statistical uncertainty of the simulation results by a factor of about 3.5.

runs.text: Why use a network to estimate a probability?
Nobody can observe "a 70% chance". You observe wins and losses, or 37 bonds in 50 trials. The network turns outcomes into a smooth probability.
No single match situation repeats often enough to count. The network shares evidence across similar situations.
In the Hagan study the network estimates were closer to the truth than the raw simulated fractions it was trained on.
Trained with 0 / 1 targets and a sigmoid or softmax output, a network estimates the probability of the class.

slides.title: Two failures, two different repairs
slides.notes: This is the central point of the hour: a training fix cannot repair a data gap.

runs.text: Train on August to November temperatures. Ask for January. The answer is absurd. Repair: add a full year of data.
Fit a noisy sine wave with 20 neurons, trained to the end. The curve wiggles through every point.
Switch on early stopping and train again. The wiggles go. Then try it on the first failure: nothing changes.
Early stopping repaired the second failure and did nothing for the first. Why?
Battery Oracle: press Break, switch on early stopping, then query outside the data.

slides.title: Try it in NeuroScape
slides.notes: The mission run is the clearest demonstration that the test set cannot reveal extrapolation.

Wiggles disappear; the out-of-range answer is flagged as not to be trusted.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.notes: A second likely question: "Explain a function approximation case study." The six-step table answers it.

runs.text: Distinguish between overfitting and extrapolation. How is each detected, and how is each prevented?
Overfitting: memorising noise; wrong between training points. Sketch the wiggly fit.
Detected by: training error low, validation and test errors much higher.
Prevented by: early stopping, regularisation, fewer neurons, more data.
Extrapolation: input outside the training range. Sketch the temperature example.
Detected by novelty detection; prevented only by data that covers the range.
